s-fc4-high-0.essay:
Audiences often remember the final door slam in Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House as a burst of freedom, as if Nora finally chooses herself over her family. But the play has been tangling those two things together since the first act. Nora's greatest act of duty, the secret loan that saved her husband's life, was also the only thing in her life that truly belonged to her. Ibsen uses this tangle to argue that obligation performed inside a dishonest home is not really obligation at all, only another role. Nora's leaving is shown as necessary, but the play deliberately keeps it from looking clean, because what she owes her children does not disappear just because her marriage was a lie.

From the start, Nora's duty and her secret freedom are the same act. Years before the play begins she forged her dying father's signature to borrow money from Krogstad so Torvald could recover in Italy. She broke the law to protect her family, and she has been quietly paying the debt by saving from her allowance and doing copying work at night. When she tells Mrs. Linde about it, she is proud, almost giddy, because it proves she is more than the "squirrel" Torvald treats her as. The irony is that her most loving sacrifice is also her rebellion. She cannot be the dutiful wife without secretly being independent, which shows that the marriage only works as long as part of Nora stays hidden.

Ibsen builds this tension through small objects and performances. The macaroons Nora sneaks and then lies about seem trivial, but they are a miniature version of the forgery: a private pleasure she has to hide from a husband who sets the rules. The tarantella in the second act takes this further. Nora dances wildly to keep Torvald away from the letterbox where Krogstad's letter sits, and Torvald coaches her steps the whole time. Her desperation looks like entertainment to him. The dance turns her real panic into a show for her husband, which is exactly what her role as wife has always required.

The climax shows why staying would not count as duty. When Torvald reads Krogstad's letter, he does not offer to take the blame the way Nora secretly hoped. He calls her a criminal and says she cannot be trusted to raise their children. Then, when a second letter returns the bond, he cheerfully forgives her. This reversal is the turning point, because Nora sees that his love depended on appearances. Her changing out of the costume into everyday clothes before their talk works as a visual signal that the performance is over. She realizes she went from being her father's doll to her husband's, so any obligation she fulfilled was really obedience.

Still, Ibsen does not let her exit feel like a simple victory. The children are left behind with Anne-Marie, the nurse who raised Nora and who once gave up her own child to do it. That detail hangs over the ending, because it suggests that women's freedom and women's sacrifice have been traded back and forth for generations. Mrs. Linde also works as a foil. She married for money to support her mother and brothers, and at the end she chooses to go back to Krogstad because she wants someone to care for. Her choice is a reminder that duty can give life meaning when it is freely chosen. Contemporary audiences found Nora's departure so disturbing that Ibsen was pressured to write an alternate ending for a German production in which she stays for the children, and he reportedly hated it. That controversy proves the play's point. Nora's leaving is meant to hurt, because Ibsen wants us to see that real obligation can only start once the self is free enough to choose it.

annotations.comment: The thesis keeps going here and sets up a line of reasoning: leaving is necessary but still costly. The body paragraphs follow this order.

s-fc4-high-1.essay:
At the end of Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, Nora Helmer walks out on her husband and three children, and the slam of the door has been argued about ever since. It is easy to read the play as a simple story of a woman escaping a bad marriage. But Ibsen makes the choice harder than that. Through Nora's secret loan, the foil characters of Mrs. Linde and the nurse Anne-Marie, and the play's unresolved ending, Ibsen suggests that Nora's duty to her family was never really a duty to them at all, but a performance she was trained to give. Her freedom is therefore both a betrayal of her children and the first honest obligation she has ever taken on, and the play refuses to let the audience feel comfortable with either half of that.

The best evidence that Nora's sense of duty is real, not just a cage, is the loan itself. Years before the play begins, she secretly borrowed money from Krogstad, forging her dead father's signature, so that Torvald could recover his health in Italy. This is an act of love and sacrifice, and she has been quietly paying it back by copying documents at night and saving from her allowance. Ironically, the one time Nora acts most dutifully as a wife, she has to break the law and act independently. Ibsen sets up a tension right away: the "doll" Torvald pets and calls his little squirrel is actually the person who saved his life. Her obligation and her freedom are already tangled together before she ever thinks of leaving.

Ibsen sharpens this with Mrs. Linde, who works almost as Nora's reverse image. Mrs. Linde gave up the man she loved, Krogstad, and married for money so she could support her sick mother and younger brothers. She did her duty completely, and it left her empty and worn out. Yet when she reunites with Krogstad, she says, in effect, that she needs someone to work for and care about. So the play doesn't treat obligation as only poison. For Mrs. Linde, choosing a commitment freely is what gives her life meaning. This matters for Nora, because it suggests that the problem was never duty in general, but duty that was handed to her without her consent.

Anne-Marie, the nurse, complicates things in a darker way. She gave up her own child to take care of Nora when Nora was small, and now she cares for Nora's children. When Nora finally leaves, she is leaving her children with a woman who already made the same sacrifice in the opposite direction. Ibsen does not let Nora's exit look clean. The freedom of one woman rests on another woman's lost family, which reminds the audience that freedom has a cost someone else pays.

The climax shows why Nora has to go anyway. She has been waiting for "the wonderful thing," expecting Torvald to take the blame for the forgery to protect her. Instead, when he reads Krogstad's letter, he panics about his reputation, and then forgives her as soon as the threat disappears. In that moment Nora sees that their marriage was a kind of play, and the tarantella she danced earlier, wild and desperate while Torvald coached her, looks like a symbol of the whole arrangement: she was performing his idea of her. Her decision to leave so she can figure out who she is reflects a duty to herself that she argues is just as sacred as her duty to her husband and children.

Still, Ibsen ends on a door, not an answer. Torvald is left hoping for a miracle, and we never learn whether Nora survives on her own or what happens to the children. That open ending is the point. A Doll's House argues that duty without self-knowledge is hollow, but it also makes us hear how loud the door is.

annotations.quote: Her freedom is therefore both a betrayal of her children and the first honest obligation she has ever taken on
annotations.comment: Defensible, specific thesis that interprets the conflict instead of restating it, and it previews a line of reasoning (the loan, foils, ending). Earns the Row A point.

annotations.quote: Ironically, the one time Nora acts most dutifully as a wife, she has to break the law and act independently.
annotations.comment: Commentary goes beyond plot summary: it uses the forged loan to show that obligation and freedom are already tangled, which ties back to the thesis.

annotations.quote: Mrs. Linde, who works almost as Nora's reverse image
annotations.comment: Uses a foil character as a literary technique and explains how it changes the meaning: duty that is freely chosen gives life meaning, duty that is imposed does not. This is the kind of linked reasoning a 4 needs.

annotations.quote: the tarantella she danced earlier, wild and desperate while Torvald coached her
annotations.comment: Reads a specific scene as a symbol of performance, so the essay looks at several elements (symbol, foil, irony, structure). Brief, but enough for the top score in Row B.

annotations.quote: The freedom of one woman rests on another woman's lost family
annotations.comment: Keeps the complexity going instead of making Nora's exit a clean win. Using Anne-Marie shows that freedom has a cost, which builds toward the sophistication point.

annotations.quote: Still, Ibsen ends on a door, not an answer.
annotations.comment: The conclusion argues that the play deliberately refuses to settle the conflict, finishing a tension the essay has followed throughout (duty as love vs. duty as performance). Because the complexity runs through the whole essay, it earns the Row C point.

s-fc4-mid-0.work_chosen: A Raisin in the Sun, Lorraine Hansberry
s-fc4-mid-0.essay:
In A Raisin in the Sun, Walter Lee Younger is pulled between his duty to his family and his desire to be a man who controls his own future. Hansberry uses this conflict to argue that real freedom cannot be separate from family and community, because when Walter tries to escape his obligations through money he ends up losing himself, and only when he chooses his family's dignity does he become free.

At the start of the play Walter sees his family as something that holds him back. He works as a chauffeur for a white man, and he resents that his mother Lena controls the insurance money from his father's death. He wants to invest in a liquor store with his friends, and he talks to his wife Ruth and his son Travis as if they do not understand how much he needs this. The cramped apartment where everyone shares a bathroom shows how the family's needs are crowding him. Walter thinks freedom means having money, and he believes his family's loyalty is what stops him from getting it.

Lena, on the other hand, represents obligation, and she uses the money to put a down payment on a house in Clybourne Park. This is a dream that comes from the whole family, not just one person. The plant that she keeps on the windowsill is a symbol of this, since she keeps caring for it even though it gets almost no sun. It shows her patience and her belief that the family can grow even in bad conditions. When Walter loses the rest of the money to his friend Willy Harris, it seems like his search for freedom has ruined everyone, and this shows the danger of choosing the self over the family.

The most important moment is when Walter is going to accept money from Mr. Lindner, who represents the neighborhood association that does not want the Youngers to move in. At first Walter seems ready to give up the family's pride for cash, which is a kind of desertion of his father's memory. But when Travis is in the room Walter cannot go through with it, and he tells Lindner that they will move. This choice is not just duty winning over freedom. Walter is free in this scene because he finally acts as the head of his family, so the two things become the same.

Hansberry does not make the ending completely happy, though. The family is moving into a hostile neighborhood, and Beneatha's dreams of becoming a doctor and the question of Asagai's proposal remain open. The play suggests that obligation can be both love and a burden, but that for the Youngers, dignity comes from facing the world together. Walter's divided loyalties show that the self is made by the family it belongs to.

annotations.quote: Hansberry uses this conflict to argue that real freedom cannot be separate from family and community
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that makes an interpretive claim about the whole play (freedom and family are linked), not just that Walter faces a hard choice. It is stated clearly, though the 'only when' phrasing is a bit broad.

annotations.quote: The cramped apartment where everyone shares a bathroom shows how the family's needs are crowding him.
annotations.comment: Specific detail of setting tied to the argument, but the commentary is brief and mostly asserts the point rather than analyzing how setting shapes meaning.

annotations.quote: The plant that she keeps on the windowsill is a symbol of this
annotations.comment: Names a specific symbol and explains what it means (patience, growth in bad conditions). This earns credit for technique, though the explanation stays fairly general and does not connect back strongly to Walter's conflict.

annotations.quote: When Walter loses the rest of the money to his friend Willy Harris
annotations.comment: Accurate plot evidence, but it leans toward summary and the link to the claim is only one sentence long, so the line of reasoning is uneven here.

annotations.quote: Walter is free in this scene because he finally acts as the head of his family, so the two things become the same.
annotations.comment: Good interpretive commentary on the Lindner scene that supports the thesis. It would be stronger with more attention to how the play's staging or dialogue builds the moment, and Travis's presence is only mentioned in passing.

annotations.quote: The play suggests that obligation can be both love and a burden
annotations.comment: Gestures at complexity and an unresolved ending (Beneatha, hostile neighborhood), but it is a short closing mention and not sustained through the essay, so it does not fully earn the sophistication point.

s-fc4-mid-1.work_chosen: A Raisin in the Sun, Lorraine Hansberry
s-fc4-mid-1.essay:
In A Raisin in the Sun, Walter Lee Younger is pulled between what he owes his family and his hunger to be his own man, and Hansberry uses this struggle to suggest that real freedom cannot be separated from duty to others. Walter only becomes free at the end of the play when he chooses his family's dignity over his own money-making dream, so the play argues that obligation, when it is chosen, can become a kind of freedom instead of just a cage.

At the start Walter sees his family as the thing holding him back. He is a chauffeur who works for another man, and he wants to invest in a liquor store with his friends. He tells Mama that she does not understand what a man needs, and he resents that the insurance money from his father's death is hers to decide about. The cramped apartment, with its worn furniture and shared bathroom, shows how the family's needs press in on him and how little room he has. Hansberry makes the setting a symbol of how duty and poverty crowd out his ambitions, which makes the audience understand why he wants out.

However, the play does not let freedom look simple. When Mama gives Walter the remaining money and tells him to put some away for Travis and Beneatha, he gives all of it to Willy Harris, who runs off with it. This is the moment where freedom turns into what could be called a quiet desertion, because Walter abandons his sister's medical school and his mother's dream in order to chase his own. Mama's plant, which she keeps trying to nurse in the sunlight, works as a contrast to Walter's choice. It shows a person who cares for something small and slow, while Walter gambles on something fast, and the contrast makes his mistake feel painful and not just foolish.

The climax is where the conflict is most complicated. Walter considers taking Mr. Lindner's offer to sell the new house back to the neighbors who do not want the Youngers there. This would solve the money problem, but it would betray his father's memory and the family's pride. In front of Travis, he refuses the offer. The fact that his son is watching matters, because it shows that Walter finally sees himself as part of a line of people and not only as an individual. He says his family is proud, and in that moment he sounds more free than at any other point, even though he is choosing the harder path of moving into a hostile neighborhood.

In the end Hansberry does not say that duty wins and the self loses. Walter's dream was always a way of taking care of his family, and his duty to them is what finally gives his dream a shape. The play shows that the self who wants freedom was formed by the very family it feels trapped by, and the move to the house is both a risk and a rescue.

annotations.quote: Walter only becomes free at the end of the play when he chooses his family's dignity over his own money-making dream
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that interprets the divided loyalty (freedom through chosen obligation) and ties it to the whole play, not just restating the prompt. Earns the thesis point, though phrasing is a bit loose.

annotations.quote: The cramped apartment, with its worn furniture and shared bathroom, shows how the family's needs press in on him
annotations.comment: Uses setting as a literary element and links it to the pull of obligation, but the detail is fairly general and the commentary stays brief.

annotations.quote: Mama's plant, which she keeps trying to nurse in the sunlight, works as a contrast to Walter's choice.
annotations.comment: Specific symbol with an explanation of how it develops meaning, a good move, but the contrast is stated rather than explored in depth.

annotations.quote: When Mama gives Walter the remaining money and tells him to put some away for Travis and Beneatha, he gives all of it to Willy Harris
annotations.comment: Accurate, specific plot evidence showing freedom as desertion, but it leans toward summary and the analysis of technique is thin.

annotations.quote: The fact that his son is watching matters, because it shows that Walter finally sees himself as part of a line of people
annotations.comment: Commentary explains how the Travis detail supports the claim, but the scene is described more than analyzed (no discussion of dialogue or staging).

annotations.quote: The play shows that the self who wants freedom was formed by the very family it feels trapped by
annotations.comment: Gestures at complexity (self formed by community, move as both risk and rescue), but it appears mainly in the conclusion and is not sustained across the essay, so it does not clearly earn sophistication.

s-fc4-low-0.work_chosen: A Raisin in the Sun, Lorraine Hansberry
s-fc4-low-0.essay:
In A Raisin in the Sun by Lorraine Hansberry, Walter Lee Younger is torn between his duty to his family and what he wants for himself. He wants to open a liquor store and be somebody, but his mother wants the family to stay together and buy a house. This is a hard choice for him and it shows how hard it is to be a Black man in Chicago at that time.

Walter's family is all living in a small apartment and everybody is crowded together. Mama gets the insurance check after Big Walter dies and she has to decide what to do with it. She puts a down payment on a house in Clybourne Park, which she thinks is good for the family. Walter is mad because he thinks she does not care about his dream. He says he wants to give his son Travis something better. This shows he feels the pull of his own wants.

Then Walter gives money to Willy Harris, who runs off with it. This is the worst moment because he lost the money that was for Beneatha's school too. Walter has failed his family because he was only thinking of himself. Mama is very upset about this and she tells him about the family.

At the end Mr. Lindner comes to pay the family not to move into the neighborhood. Walter almost takes the money but he decides not to, and says they will move. This shows that he chooses his family and his pride over the money. The family moves out of the apartment and Mama takes her plant with her.

In conclusion, Walter is caught between family and freedom and in the end he chooses his family. The play shows that family duty is important and that dreams can be hard to reach.

annotations.quote: Walter Lee Younger is torn between his duty to his family and what he wants for himself.
annotations.comment: This only restates the prompt's idea of being torn. It states that a conflict exists but offers no interpretation of what the play as a whole means, so the thesis point is not earned.

annotations.quote: This is a hard choice for him and it shows how hard it is to be a Black man in Chicago at that time.
annotations.comment: This is a general comment about difficulty, not a defensible claim about how the divided loyalties shape the work's meaning. It also lacks any link to specific evidence.

annotations.quote: She puts a down payment on a house in Clybourne Park, which she thinks is good for the family.
annotations.comment: This is accurate plot summary. It names a real event but does not explain how it develops an argument or what the house symbolizes, so it earns little under evidence and commentary.

annotations.quote: This shows he feels the pull of his own wants.
annotations.comment: This commentary is vague and repeats the prompt. It does not analyze Walter's dialogue or any literary technique, so it does not explain how the evidence supports a claim.

annotations.quote: Walter has failed his family because he was only thinking of himself.
annotations.comment: This oversimplifies the conflict by treating Walter's dream as mere selfishness. It ignores that his ambition is also tied to providing for Travis, so the commentary is thin and one-sided.

annotations.quote: This shows that he chooses his family and his pride over the money.
annotations.comment: The Lindner scene is the right evidence, but the essay only retells it. It does not analyze what the refusal means for the play's view of dignity or freedom, and it does not mention technique.

annotations.quote: The play shows that family duty is important and that dreams can be hard to reach.
annotations.comment: This conclusion is a generic claim that treats duty and freedom as separate and resolved in favor of family. It does not explore the tension, the historical context of housing discrimination, or any ambiguity in the ending, so sophistication is not shown.

s-fc4-low-1.essay:
In A Doll's House by Henrik Ibsen, Nora is torn between what she owes her family and what she wants for herself. This is a hard choice for her and it shows up all through the play. In the end she makes a choice and the play shows what happens because of it.

At the start Nora seems like a happy wife. She is called names like "little squirrel" by her husband Torvald and she acts like a child, eating macaroons when he tells her not to. She does what her family wants because she thinks that is what a good wife does. But she also has a secret, because she borrowed money to save Torvald's life when he was sick, and she forged her father's name to get it. This shows that she has done something for her family but also did it on her own, which is a kind of freedom.

Later in the play Krogstad threatens to tell Torvald about the loan. Nora is very scared and she practices the tarantella dance harder and harder. The dance shows how she is feeling because it is wild and she is trapped. Torvald finds the letter and gets angry at her instead of thanking her, and he says she has ruined his happiness. This is when Nora sees that her marriage was not what she thought.

Finally Nora leaves her husband and children and slams the door. Many people at the time were shocked by this. She says she has to find out who she is. So the play shows that Nora had a duty to her family but she had to leave to be herself. The ending is sad but also hopeful, and it shows that freedom and duty are both important but sometimes you have to pick.

annotations.quote: Nora is torn between what she owes her family and what she wants for herself.
annotations.comment: Restates the prompt and says only that Nora faces a conflict. No defensible interpretation of the whole work, so no thesis point.

annotations.quote: So the play shows that Nora had a duty to her family but she had to leave to be herself.
annotations.comment: Closest thing to a claim, but it comes at the end and is a summary of her decision, not an interpretation that could be argued.

annotations.quote: she forged her father's name to get it
annotations.comment: Accurate, specific detail, but it is retold as plot and the link to freedom versus duty is only asserted, not explained.

annotations.quote: The dance shows how she is feeling because it is wild and she is trapped.
annotations.comment: Attempts to read a symbol, but the commentary is general and does not show how the tarantella develops meaning about obligation and freedom.

annotations.quote: The ending is sad but also hopeful, and it shows that freedom and duty are both important but sometimes you have to pick.
annotations.comment: Gestures at tension but in a general, one-sentence way. It never explores the cost of leaving the children or how the home shaped Nora, so complexity is not developed.
